question: What is the primary cause of an ischemic stroke?

options.A: Trauma to the skull and brain
options.B: A blocked blood vessel from a clot

explanation: Ischemic strokes happen when a thrombus or embolus blocks blood flow inside a cerebral artery. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h1)

question: Why is hypertension a major risk factor for hemorrhagic stroke?

options.A: It thickens the blood and slows down circulation
options.B: It causes blood clots to form quickly in the heart
options.C: It shrinks the brain tissue inside the skull
options.D: It puts constant high pressure on weak vessel walls

explanation: Chronic high blood pressure weakens arterial walls over time, making them prone to bursting and bleeding into the brain. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h1)

question: A stroke in the right cerebral hemisphere typically causes weakness on which part of the body?
explanation: Motor pathways cross over in the brainstem, meaning injury to one hemisphere affects the contralateral side of the body. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h2)

question: A patient with left-hemisphere stroke damage is most likely to exhibit which symptom?

options.A: Loss of balance when sitting upright
options.B: Total disregard for the left side of space
options.C: Severe difficulty with speech and language

explanation: The left hemisphere houses language centers like Broca's and Wernicke's areas in most individuals. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h2)

question: What does the term 'learned nonuse' mean in stroke recovery?

options.A: Ignoring the weak limb and relying only on the good side
options.B: Inability to remember basic daily routines
options.C: Forgetting how to walk due to lack of exercise
options.D: Refusing to take prescribed daily medications

explanation: Learned nonuse develops when a patient stops trying to use the affected arm or leg because initial attempts are difficult. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h3)

question: How can a nurse best promote independence during morning care for a stroke patient?

options.A: Wait until family members arrive to assist
options.B: Encourage the patient to do as much as possible alone
options.C: Complete all tasks quickly so the patient can rest
options.D: Feed and bathe the patient to prevent fatigue

explanation: Active participation in daily tasks builds muscle strength, motor planning, and psychological confidence. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h3)

question: What is spasticity characterized by in stroke survivors?

options.A: Sudden loss of sensation in the lower limbs
options.C: Involuntary muscle stiffness and increased tone
options.D: Complete limpness of the affected muscles

explanation: Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone caused by upper motor neuron damage. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h4)

question: A stroke patient with left-sided weakness is ready to transfer from the bed to a chair. Where should the nurse place the chair?

options.A: Directly facing the foot of the bed
options.B: On the patient's strong right side
options.C: On the patient's weak left side
options.D: At a distance requiring a short run

explanation: Transferring toward the strong side allows the patient to weight-bear and control movement with their stronger limbs. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h4)

question: A patient with expressive aphasia struggles most with which ability?

options.A: Understanding spoken questions from the nurse
options.C: Reading written instructions on a chart
options.D: Speaking or finding the right words to say

explanation: Expressive aphasia leaves comprehension intact while making verbal output difficult or halting. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h5)

question: What is the best communication approach when caring for a patient with severe receptive aphasia?

options.A: Write long paragraphs explaining every procedure
options.B: Speak very loudly and quickly to catch attention
options.C: Rely entirely on complex medical terminology
options.D: Use gestures, simple words, and visual aids

explanation: Receptive aphasia impairs spoken word comprehension, so visual cues and simple language help bridge the gap. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h5)

question: Which complication is most directly linked to swallowing difficulties after a stroke?

options.B: Deep vein thrombosis in the calf

explanation: Dysphagia allows food or liquid to enter the airway, leading to bacterial lung infection known as aspiration pneumonia. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h6)

question: How can a home health nurse help prevent pressure injuries in a bedridden stroke patient?

options.A: Apply thick lotion to the skin every ten minutes
options.B: Turn and reposition the patient every two hours
options.C: Limit fluid intake to reduce skin moisture
options.D: Keep the head of the bed elevated at 90 degrees

explanation: Regular repositioning relieves pressure on vulnerable skin areas, restoring blood flow and preventing tissue breakdown. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h6)

question: What is a frequent negative outcome experienced by long-term stroke family caregivers?

options.A: Permanent hearing loss from high noise levels
options.C: Sudden loss of their own motor function

explanation: The continuous demands of assisting a dependent survivor often lead to severe physical and psychological strain. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h7)

question: Why is educating the family caregiver on safe body mechanics vital during home visits?

options.A: To speed up the healing of brain tissue damage
options.B: To ensure the patient learns how to walk independently
options.C: To prevent injury to the caregiver while lifting the patient
options.D: To eliminate the need for any future medical checkups

explanation: Caregivers often hurt their own backs and joints when transferring heavy, immobile patients without proper technique. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T9#GNS324_U4_T9_h7)
